links.note: The Lutheran Formula of Concord of 1577 lists the 'Erroneous Articles of the Schwenckfeldians'. It rejects their teaching that Christ's glorified flesh took on all divine properties. It also rejects their view that the water of baptism is not a means by which God works new birth.
links.outcome_considered: The Formula is a confession of faith. None of the listed lines shows a council, law or ruler's act enforcing it against the Schwenckfelders.

Grading: Trent's canon does not name the Anabaptists, and the courts that killed them (Ensisheim, Sattler's Rottenburg trial) were Habsburg civil courts, not the Church itself. I graded Documented because the canon condemns their defining teaching word for word and the martyr book names them as the persecuted. A reviewer could reasonably take this to Widely Accepted; no repo-cited secondary for that reading has been read, so I did not.
The Ensisheim figure is the Martyrs Mirror's report of Sebastian Franck's chronicle (1660 compilation), not a court record. Sattler's sentence is the compilation's text of the 1527 account.
'bap tism' (line break without hyphen) and 'Ensis- heim' are kept as the file prints them.

links.note: Scholars disagree about how much the English Baptists owed the Anabaptists. John Smyth's church in exile baptized its own members anew in Amsterdam. Then Smyth asked to join the Mennonite church there. He called his own new baptism an error. Thomas Helwys and his party kept theirs.
links.outcome: The question split Smyth's church in Amsterdam in about 1609. His party sought to join the Mennonites. Helwys's party kept apart and later founded the General Baptists.

prose_changes.old: Grew out of late-medieval piety and its protest against Rome, becoming a rival to Rome and a sibling rival to the Reformed churches. The Augustinian Hermits, Luther's own religious order, were its seedbed: the order's houses in Lutheran lands were absorbed into the new movement, while its Catholic houses continued within the Catholic Church.
prose_changes.new: It began in 1517, when one friar spoke out against the sale of indulgences. Luther also drew on an old German mystical book, the Theologia Deutsch. The movement became a rival to Rome, and a sibling rival to the Reformed churches. Many friars of Luther's own order were among his first followers.
prose_changes.reason: 'Grew out of late-medieval piety' was vague and the inventory tied it to an English parish movement; replaced by the documented Theologia Deutsch reception. The Augustinian houses' being 'absorbed' or 'continued' is not in any vendored text; qualified to what the 1931 editor's note in the Luther works shows. Whole field rewritten for reading level.

prose_changes.old: Parent of the Scottish, Huguenot, Dutch, and Puritan traditions
prose_changes.new: Zurich and Geneva shaped the Scottish, Huguenot, Dutch and Puritan traditions.

prose_changes.old: Reformed and Presbyterian churches worldwide descend from these two cities, and so do four traditions this map carries separately. The Scottish Kirk, the Huguenots, the Dutch Reformed and English Puritanism. Beyond doctrine the everyday inheritance is a style: plain whitewashed interiors with the pulpit at the center, congregational psalm-singing in the language people spoke, and church government by elected elders rather than by bishops.
prose_changes.new: Reformed and Presbyterian churches around the world descend from these two cities. Four traditions shown on their own on this map took their pattern from them. They are the Scottish Kirk, the Huguenots, the Dutch Reformed and English Puritanism. Beyond belief, the everyday heritage is a style. The churches are plain and whitewashed, with the pulpit in the middle. Whole congregations sing the psalms in their own tongue. And elected elders lead the church, not bishops.
prose_changes.reason: 'So do four traditions' (descent) qualified to 'took their pattern from them', matching the links. The stray sentence fragment is joined. Whole field rewritten for reading level, keeping its images.

prose_changes.old: Persecuted by Lutheran, Reformed, and Catholic traditions alike - a loud tension in the sources; parent of the free-church line
prose_changes.new: Lutheran, Reformed and Catholic churches all condemned them. Catholic lands hunted them hardest. They led the way for the free churches that came later, such as the Baptists.
prose_changes.reason: 'Persecuted by Lutheran ... alike' outruns the sources for the Lutheran side; 'a loud tension in the sources' was build commentary; 'parent' of the free churches is contested (the Baptists' own text says so).

prose_changes.old: In January 1525 a handful of men in Zurich, impatient with how slowly their own city's reform was moving, baptized one another as adults — and were hunted for it. Anabaptists held that baptism belonged to those who could confess faith for themselves, that the church was a voluntary body rather than a whole society, and, for most of them, that a Christian could neither swear oaths nor take up the sword. Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed authorities alike treated this as sedition and executed them by the hundreds. The survivors regrouped: Hutterite communities holding goods in common in Moravia, and in the Low Countries the congregations gathered by a former priest, Menno Simons, whose name their descendants still carry.
prose_changes.new: In January 1525 a handful of men in Zurich baptized one another as adults. They were impatient with how slowly their own city's reform was moving, and they were hunted for it. Anabaptists held that baptism belonged to those who could confess faith for themselves. The church, they said, was a free body of believers, not a whole society. Most of them also held that a Christian could neither swear oaths nor take up the sword. Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed rulers alike saw them as a threat to order. By one early count more than two thousand were put to death, above all in Catholic lands. The survivors regrouped. In Moravia, Hutterite communities held their goods in common. In the Low Countries, a former priest named Menno Simons gathered congregations, and their descendants still carry his name.
prose_changes.reason: 'Executed them by the hundreds' laid on all three alike; no vendored text shows Lutheran executions. Now the Martyrs Mirror's count (citing Franck), tied to Catholic lands; Zurich's executions are carried by the rewritten link. Whole field rewritten for reading level.

prose_changes.old: In January 1525, a small group in Zurich baptized one another as adults, and Lutheran, Reformed and Catholic authorities alike hunted them down for it. What survives from inside the movement is unusually direct: court testimony, prison hymns and a martyr book, the Martyrs Mirror, still read aloud in Amish and Mennonite homes today.
prose_changes.new: In January 1525, a small group in Zurich baptized one another as adults. Lutheran, Reformed and Catholic leaders alike condemned them for it. What survives from inside the movement is rare and direct. Trial papers survive, and so do prison hymns and a book of martyrs. That book, the Martyrs Mirror, is still read aloud in Amish and Mennonite homes.
prose_changes.reason: 'Hunted them down' is not shown for the Lutheran side; now 'condemned them'. Whole field rewritten for reading level.

prose_changes.old: The movement survives directly: Mennonites, Amish, Hutterites and Brethren all descend from it, and the wider free-church principle — that membership is a voluntary adult commitment and that the church should not be an arm of the state — became one of the most widely adopted Protestant ideas in the world. Its martyr book, the Martyrs Mirror of 1660, is still printed and still read aloud in Amish and Mennonite homes.
prose_changes.new: The movement survives directly. Mennonites, Amish and Hutterites descend from it, and the later Brethren drew on its beliefs. Its free-church idea also spread far beyond it. Joining a church is a free choice made as an adult, and the church should not be an arm of the state. That became one of the most widely shared Protestant ideas in the world. Its martyr book, the Martyrs Mirror of 1660, is still printed and still read aloud in Amish and Mennonite homes.
prose_changes.reason: 'Brethren ... descend from it' is what the Brethren historian Brumbaugh rejects; now 'drew on its convictions', matching the link. Whole field rewritten for reading level.

prose_changes.new: Perhaps a quiet influence on later dissent, though their secrecy hides the trail.
prose_changes.reason: No source traces the influence; stated as uncertain, with the reason the movement's own text gives.

prose_changes.old: Neither group survived as an institution. Franck's writings, though, were read and reprinted for centuries by people looking for a Christianity without an institution, and reached the later mystical and spiritualist strands of Protestantism. The Familists' habit of outward conformity makes their influence almost impossible to trace — which is exactly what they intended — but their books circulated among Dutch printers and English readers, and the arguments for toleration made in the following century drew on that Christian tradition.
prose_changes.new: Neither group lasted as an institution. Franck's writings, though, were reprinted long after his death. They found readers who wanted a Christian faith without a church to house it. His Paradoxa came out again in 1559, and an English version of another of his books in 1640. They may have reached later mystics and spiritualists, but that path is hard to trace. The Familists' habit of outward conformity hides their influence almost completely. That is exactly what they wanted. Their books were printed abroad in English for English readers, and one was reprinted in London as late as 1652. Whether they fed the next century's case for toleration cannot be shown.
prose_changes.reason: Three claims outran the sources: Franck's writings 'reached' later spiritualists, 'Dutch printers', and the toleration arguments 'drew on' the tradition. Each is now stated as far as the vendored prints go. Whole field rewritten for reading level.
